ami_style_notes:
The meeting has a casual, collegial video-call style, with mostly short-to-medium turns in the opening social chat and much longer, structured presentation turns once talks begin. Overlap and interruptions are low during formal remarks but common in transitions, greetings, and question exchanges, where speakers jump in with “yeah,” “okay,” or brief acknowledgments. Participants use frequent hedging and self-repair—“um,” “I think,” “sort of,” “you know,” “maybe,” repeated words, and restarted phrases—giving the discussion an informal, spontaneous feel. Formality is moderate: introductions and thanks are polished but conversational, while questions are often prefaced as “quick,” “naive,” or “good” questions. Challenges are indirect and collaborative, framed as extensions, uncertainties, or requests for clarification rather than blunt disagreement. Speakers build on prior comments by restating part of the point, offering related evidence, and inviting follow-up; answers tend to be expansive, qualified, and open about limitations.

Meeting style for this meeting (running_out_of_time): The meeting starts late or the agenda is too long. People keep an eye on the clock, cut themselves off, skip items, and the meeting ends with things unfinished. No final recap.
Illustration of the feel only (invented, do not reuse the wording or topic):
  - We've got maybe fifteen minutes, so- can we skip the intro stuff?
  - Yeah, sure. Let's just start with what's blocking.
  - I really have to jump in about five, sorry.
Opening: Start mid-thought, as if the conversation was already under way before the recording started.
Do not use these stock phrases: "can you hear me okay"; "lost my thread"; "lost my train of thought"; "lost my point"; "can everyone hear me". The recording does not need to begin with audio or login checks.
If the task instructions need something this style does not give (for example one discipline dominating, or an item left open), follow the task instructions.
research_problem: Working out why wild bee numbers on farms did not recover after wildflower strips were planted along field edges.

speakers.name: Dr. Maya Chen
speakers.background: A third-year ecology PhD student coordinating the 18-farm field protocol. Her work combines repeated transect and pan-trap surveys, GIS-based measures of semi-natural habitat and strip connectivity, and field assessments of floral continuity and nesting substrates. She has two seasons of experience working with farm advisers and land managers on agri-environment monitoring.
speakers.distinct_perspective: Chen treats the lack of a count response as a scale-and-resource problem rather than evidence that strips failed outright. She wants to distinguish local floral provision from landscape permeability, nesting limitation, and seasonal gaps in forage, while recognizing that detectability and weather can obscure real changes. She is especially focused on translating farm-specific management histories into defensible sampling priorities for the April surveys.
speakers.language_complexity: moderate — balances jargon with accessible language
speakers.epistemic_stance: uncertain about how their methods apply to this problem

speakers.name: Dr. Luis Romero
speakers.background: A pollinator biologist with 14 years of experience in wild-bee taxonomy, functional-trait analysis, and pesticide-exposure research. He has led regional reference-collection work and uses morphology, DNA barcoding where needed, pollen residue data, and species-specific foraging-range estimates to interpret exposure and habitat use. He is coordinating identification, voucher procedures, and exposure measures for the study.
speakers.distinct_perspective: Romero argues that aggregate bee counts may conceal contrasting species-level responses: a strip can benefit small-bodied generalists while failing to support specialists or bees constrained by nesting habitat and pesticide exposure. He emphasizes matching interpretations of field-edge resources and pesticide timing to the likely movement ranges, phenology, and life histories of identified taxa. He probes whether the planned sampling can separate sublethal effects from changes in floral attraction or detectability.
speakers.language_complexity: moderate — balances jargon with accessible language
speakers.epistemic_stance: uncertain about how their methods apply to this problem

speakers.name: Dr. Priya Shah
speakers.background: An agricultural economist with 11 years of experience evaluating agri-environment schemes, farm budgets, and land-manager decision-making. She has designed mixed-methods studies using semi-structured interviews, enterprise-level cost accounting, subsidy-policy analysis, and stated management histories. She is coordinating the interview instruments, farm-budget component, and liaison schedule across participating farms.
speakers.distinct_perspective: Shah frames strip outcomes partly as the result of implementation incentives and operational constraints. She is interested in whether seed mixes, mowing, reseeding, pesticide timing, and edge management reflect subsidy conditions, cash-flow pressures, labor availability, or perceived crop-yield risk rather than simple noncompliance. She wants interview evidence to make the ecological measures interpretable at farm level, while remaining ready to revise economic assumptions if biological mechanisms better explain observed patterns.
speakers.language_complexity: moderate — balances jargon with accessible language
speakers.epistemic_stance: open to other perspectives, willing to revise

transcript.speaker: Dr. Maya Chen
transcript.text: —before we get into it, I’ve had two of the farm contacts ask whether April dates are fixed yet, so I think we need to leave today with at least a route to getting access windows and weather backup dates. Mainly, though, I’d like us to pin down what the interviews can realistically tell the field protocol before I lock the management-history form and the farm-specific sampling priorities.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Luis Romero
transcript.text: Mm, yes, timing is tight.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Priya Shah
transcript.text: —the interviews can give you usable information, but only if we separate what actually changes a sampling decision from what is just explanatory context. Maya, which management details do we need for that distinction? And Luis, for pesticide exposure, how much detail on the product, timing, and where it was applied is it actually worth asking farmers to reconstruct?

transcript.speaker: Dr. Luis Romero
transcript.text: For exposure, I'd ask for the product, the date or at least the week, which crop and field were treated, the application method, and whether a contractor applied it. What we need is something we can line up with each survey date and the activity window of the taxa, not just a general account of a spray programme. Priya, in your previous interviews, how precise have those records been, especially when a contractor applied it...

transcript.speaker: Dr. Priya Shah
transcript.text: For contractor applications, the records can be- it’s often pretty patchy. Managers may have invoices or a spray log, but not the product detail to hand in an interview. I’d ask them to identify the contractor and say whether records can be shared or checked afterwards, rather than press them to recall it. And we should allow a week-level date where that’s all they can substantiate.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Maya Chen
transcript.text: That’s helpful. For the form, I think we can make the date field week-level, then flag records that are invoice- or log-verified instead of pretending we have precision we don’t. Priya, for mowing and reseeding, what have managers actually been able to recall reliably, especially whether it happened before or during the main flowering window?

transcript.speaker: Dr. Luis Romero
transcript.text: Right, and the flowering window matters.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Priya Shah
transcript.text: On the liaison calls, people can usually place mowing against a crop stage or a holiday period more reliably than they can give a date. I'd ask if it was before first bloom, during peak flowering, or after flowering, and then record the approximate week if they have it. Reseeding is less consistently recalled, so I'd want seed invoices or scheme records where possible. Maya, is that flowering-stage distinction enough for your priorities?

transcript.speaker: Dr. Maya Chen
transcript.text: I think that's enough to set priorities. If mowing was during peak flower, we'd- if it happened during peak flower, we'll add an early revisit, or at least treat the floral assessment differently, rather than assume the strip is comparable all season. For reseeding, a verified record matters more for interpreting establishment than for changing an April transect, probably. Luis, on your side, which species or trait groups would actually make you change the exposure radius or survey timing farm by farm?

transcript.speaker: Dr. Luis Romero
transcript.text: I wouldn't set a unique radius for every taxon, that becomes unworkable. But if early identifications show mostly small-bodied Andrena or Lasioglossum, I'd weight the immediately adjacent fields and strip condition much more heavily. If we have Bombus or larger cavity-nesters, the relevant landscape and, and potential spray sources extend further. Survey timing should cover the early spring specialists as well as the mid-season generalists, otherwise the apparent non-response could just be a shift in who's present.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Priya Shah
transcript.text: —and that makes the sequencing awkward: interviews are meant to start February 1, but ethics approval is not expected until March 1. We cannot use interview evidence to finalise April priorities on the current timetable, unless that approval date moves.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Maya Chen
transcript.text: —then we may need a provisional April core protocol that doesn’t depend on interviews, and only use any early returns to flag additions. Otherwise I can’t make farm-specific changes fairly across all 18. Is there any route to speaking about access without collecting research interview data?

transcript.speaker: Dr. Priya Shah
transcript.text: I think so, provided we keep it operational. A brief contact to confirm access windows, the appropriate site contact, and whether there are any known restrictions in April. I’d want the consent-facing wording checked before we send even that, because questions about management or, um, the reasons for restrictions could drift into research data quite quickly.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Maya Chen
transcript.text: —that works for me. If we keep the access contact to windows, the named contact, and weather-contingency availability, I can build the provisional routes without touching management history. I just need to know whether every farm can offer a backup visit, because otherwise the repeated surveys stop being comparable pretty quickly.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Priya Shah
transcript.text: I can separate that operational contact from the interview workflow and make the boundary explicit. It would just cover access dates, backup availability, site contact, and restrictions only, no management questions. I’m a little concerned that a restriction can itself imply spraying or mowing, so perhaps the form just records that there is a restriction and, and leaves the reason blank until consent is in place.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Maya Chen
transcript.text: Leave the reason blank, that keeps it clean. For routing, if there's a restriction and we don't know why, that's still enough for me to know we might need a different visit order or a backup date. I don't need to infer why. I would like the operational form to ask whether the restriction affects access to the strip itself or just a field edge, though, because that changes whether we can keep the transect and pan-trap placement comparable.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Luis Romero
transcript.text: For the biological work, I'd add whether the restriction keeps us out of the strip or just changes the route to it. If we have to move the pan traps or the transect, we need to record that as a placement change, not just an access note, because it could change which taxa we detect.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Priya Shah
transcript.text: I’ll add that distinction and keep it strictly descriptive. Access to the strip, access only by an alternative route, or access to neither. And I’ll include a field for whether the agreed placement would need to move. I was going to ask what caused it, but no, we won’t ask that. Then Maya and Luis can treat it as a protocol deviation rather than a management-history observation.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Maya Chen
transcript.text: Yeah, exactly. If it does have to move, I need the original intended location and the replacement marked on the field map, even if the move is only ten metres, so we can separate a genuine farm difference from a placement issue later. I’ll keep the April core transect and pan-trap layout fixed otherwise; there isn’t really time now to make interview-led redesigns across all 18.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Priya Shah
transcript.text: —good. I’ll build those map fields into the operational contact, and I’ll keep the management-history module entirely separate until approval is in place. One thing I still need to check is whether our budget template can actually separate establishment from recurrent maintenance when labour is recorded as informal hand work or machinery detours. The calls so far suggest the payment-covered costs and the costs managers experience are- they’re not lining up.
